components.title: Motivation and Core Architecture of Model Context Protocols
components.teaches: Explain why standardized context protocols are required to decouple LLM clients from disparate external tools and data sources. Students will understand the client-host-server topology and how it solves the M×N integration bottleneck compared to bespoke API integrations.

components.title: JSON-RPC Message Framing and Transport Layer Mechanisms
components.teaches: Examine the transport mechanisms used to exchange messages between hosts and context servers, focusing on standard input/output (stdio) and Server-Sent Events (SSE) over HTTP. Students will identify how JSON-RPC 2.0 framing is used to structure requests, responses, and notifications across these transports.

components.title: Protocol Initialization Handshake and Capability Negotiation
components.teaches: Trace the step-by-step lifecycle of protocol initialization, including the client 'initialize' request, server response, and initialized notification. Students will analyze how client and server negotiate supported capabilities such as tools, prompts, resources, and experimental extensions.

components.title: Comparing Local stdio and Remote SSE Deployment Architectures
components.teaches: Compare the operational and architectural trade-offs between local stdio subprocesses and remote SSE network services. Students will evaluate factors such as local process isolation, network latency, authentication challenges, and persistence requirements.

components.title: Recap of Protocol Lifecycles and Core Primitives
components.teaches: Summarize the JSON-RPC initialization handshake and introduce the three core MCP primitives: resources, prompts, and tools. Students will distinguish between passive data provision (resources) and dynamic model operations (tools).

components.title: Defining Resources and Resource Templates in Context Schemas
components.teaches: Explain how context servers expose data via URI schemes and parameterized resource templates. Students will identify the schema fields used to define static text/binary content, MIME types, and dynamic URI-based subscription updates.

components.title: Tool Definitions and Dynamic Execution Callbacks
components.teaches: Examine how servers declare executable tools using JSON Schema for input argument validation. Students will follow the flow from tool discovery (`tools/list`) through host invocation (`tools/call`) to returning structured execution results or errors.

components.title: Developer Workspace Configuration Schemas and Server Registration
components.teaches: Break down the structure of workspace configuration files, such as `mcpServers` sections in desktop or IDE configuration files. Students will identify mandatory fields including command, args, env variables, and transport settings required to launch context servers.

components.title: Security Boundaries, Environment Isolation, and Access Control
components.teaches: Analyze security risks associated with granting language models access to local files and CLI execution via context protocols. Students will identify mitigation strategies, including sandboxed subprocess execution, prompt injection defense in tool outputs, and explicit user-in-the-loop approvals.

components.title: Inspecting Configuration Templates for Model Context Protocols
components.teaches: Walk through a supplied developer workspace template to identify configured context servers, missing schema fields, and transport definitions. Students will pinpoint configuration discrepancies such as misconfigured PATHs, missing environment variables, or schema type mismatches.

components.title: Diagnosing Protocol Connection Failures and Logging Workflows
components.teaches: Demonstrate how to detect and trace common protocol runtime errors using client diagnostic logs and server error codes. Students will evaluate stderr streams, malformed JSON-RPC payloads, and unhandled transport disconnects.

components.title: Evolution from Traditional to AI-Augmented Developer Workflows
components.teaches: Understand how software development lifecycles transition from manual writing and manual searching to AI-augmented authoring. Identify the shift from linear edit-compile-debug loops to continuous speculative drafting and prompt refinement. Explain the fundamental expectations and boundaries of integrating language models into active development environments.

components.title: Core Architectural Components of Modern AI Code Assistants
components.teaches: Identify the primary software building blocks connecting an editor to an underlying generative model. Detail how client-side plugins gather telemetry, local buffers, and cursor positions before transmitting them through an orchestrator to an inference engine. Recognize the responsibilities of the local extension versus remote inference endpoints.

components.title: Context Retrieval and Window Slicing in AI Assistants
components.teaches: Understand how AI assistants extract active file snippets, open tabs, and recent terminal outputs to populate an inference prompt. Examine how context budgets limit input tokens and how sliding windows prioritize lines surrounding the current cursor position. Describe the trade-offs between local context breadth and token latency during autocomplete generation.

components.title: Contextualisation Guidelines for Scoped Code Generation Tasks
components.teaches: Identify and apply core contextualisation guidelines to constrain AI prompts for short coding items such as utility functions, docstrings, and unit tests. Explain why providing explicit type signatures, interfaces, and minimal reproducible input-output examples produces deterministic code. Distinguish between over-contextualised prompts that exhaust token limits and under-contextualised prompts that cause generic completions.

components.title: Interaction Modalities: Ghost Text, Chat, and Inline Edits
components.teaches: Compare the operational patterns of in-line ghost-text autocompletion, docked conversational sidebars, and targeted in-line refactoring. Analyze when a developer should rely on passive inline completion versus active conversational elicitation for complex logic. Identify the cognitive load and interruption costs associated with each interaction modality.

components.title: Demonstration of Context Feeding in an AI-Assisted IDE
components.teaches: Observe how an AI coding assistant dynamically alters suggested code based on open editor tabs, language server protocol (LSP) diagnostics, and active comments. Follow the step-by-step transformation of a prompt payload when new files are opened or relevant interfaces are imported. Recognize how real-time IDE state changes directly manipulate model generation outcomes.

components.title: Common Failure Modes: Hallucination and Stale Context in Workflows
components.teaches: Examine concrete examples where AI assistants hallucinate deprecated API methods, fabricate package dependencies, or carry stale context across branch switches. Analyze how incomplete context retrieval leads to syntactically valid yet logically flawed code snippets. Identify the risks of silent degradation in code quality when developers accept completions without manual inspection.

components.title: Verification Strategies and Quality Gates for AI-Assisted Code
components.teaches: Evaluate verification techniques necessary to safely assimilate AI-generated snippets into professional codebases. Discuss the role of automated linting, localized test suites, and strict human review protocols as immediate guardrails. Formulate guidelines for establishing developer responsibility when committing code drafted with generative models.

components.title: Anatomy of coding agent workspaces and execution lifecycle
components.teaches: Students will understand the core architectural layers of an autonomous coding agent workspace, including environment virtualization, state tracking, and scratchpad management. They will trace how an agent transitions from prompt ingestion to planning, tool dispatch, and observation intake.

components.title: Context engineering strategies for constrained context windows
components.teaches: Students will learn context engineering mechanisms such as selective file tree pruning, sliding context windows, and dynamic relevance filtering. They will evaluate trade-offs between full repository indexing and lightweight context token budgets to prevent model distraction.

components.title: Structuring MCP tool schemas and workspace descriptors
components.teaches: Students will learn how to structure tool definitions using Model Context Protocol (MCP) JSON schemas so agents can discover and invoke workspace tools cleanly. They will specify required arguments, return payloads, and environment permissions according to MCP interface specifications.

components.title: Evaluating context pollution and tool discovery trade-offs
components.teaches: Students will analyse the failure modes caused by context pollution when exposing too many MCP tools or verbose tool definitions to a coding agent. They will compare lazy tool registration against global tool injection in terms of latency, token cost, and hallucinated invocations.

components.title: Static analysis constraints on agent tool configurations
components.teaches: Students will identify common static analyser warnings and strict schema violations that arise when registering MCP server endpoints. They will review rule sets for configuration linters, strict typing of input parameters, and required metadata tags.

components.title: Configuring custom MCP tool manifests and execution environments
components.teaches: Students will write and configure MCP server manifest files to expose custom tools (such as git, linters, or test runners) directly inside an agent workspace. They will configure environment variables, working directory permissions, and execution sandboxes to ensure deterministic agent actions.

components.title: Validating workspace tool configurations against test suites
components.teaches: Students will walk through setting up and running public integration test suites and static analysis tools against an MCP-integrated agent workspace. They will remediate schema mismatches and failing integration tests until the agent configuration passes cleanly without warnings.

components.title: Diagnosing runtime tool configuration failures in agent workflows
components.teaches: Students will examine real-world case studies where subtle tool configuration errors—such as malformed error responses or improper argument defaults—caused an agent to enter infinite loops or crash. They will identify the root cause in the tool manifest and describe how robust configuration prevents runtime divergence.

M2.T2.topic: Custom tool integrations using model context protocols

components.title: Architecture of Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients and servers
components.teaches: Students will understand the client-server architecture of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and how LLM agent workspaces communicate with external tools. They will identify the roles of host applications, MCP clients, and MCP servers during session initialization and tool exposure.

components.title: JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol format for tool discovery and calls
components.teaches: Students will learn how JSON-RPC 2.0 messages are structured for tools/list and tools/call requests in MCP. They will examine request IDs, method headers, parameter payloads, and response objects transmitted over standard streams.

components.title: Defining strict input JSON schemas for MCP tools
components.teaches: Students will learn how to write precise JSON Schema definitions for tool parameters to guide LLM tool calling. They will specify required fields, parameter data types, descriptions, and validation constraints that prevent ambiguous agent invocations.

components.title: Implementing an MCP server using an official SDK
components.teaches: Students will walk through building a lightweight MCP server using an official SDK. They will observe how decorated functions are exposed as callable tools and how incoming JSON arguments are parsed automatically.

components.title: Activity: Writing and running a custom MCP server tool
components.teaches: Students will write a custom tool function on an MCP server that executes local file or system operations and returns formatted content blocks. They will test the server execution using standard input streams to verify correct responses.

components.title: Configuring workspace settings to discover custom MCP servers
components.teaches: Students will configure an agent workspace JSON configuration file to register their custom server executable and command-line arguments. They will verify that the agent successfully discovers and surfaces the new tool capabilities.

components.title: Handling execution errors and returning structured MCP errors
components.teaches: Students will learn how to catch internal tool execution failures and map them to structured MCP error responses using the isError flag. They will distinguish between runtime exceptions inside tool execution and protocol-level transport failures.

components.title: Static analysis and linter rules for safe MCP server code
components.teaches: Students will configure static analysis tools to validate type safety, async patterns, and error handling in custom MCP server implementations. They will identify common static analyser warnings related to untyped JSON schema bindings and unhandled promises.

components.title: Activity: Passing automated MCP tool test suites without warnings
components.teaches: Students will run integration test suites against their configured MCP tool integration in an agent workspace environment. They will fix failing test cases and resolve all static analysis warnings to ensure production-grade tool configuration.

M3.T1.topic: Standards and specification guidelines for use cases

components.title: The Need for Standardized Use Case Specifications
components.teaches: Students will understand why unstructured product descriptions lead to scope creep and misinterpretation in software projects. They will identify standard use case components necessary for transforming raw ideas into precise functional specifications.

components.title: Defining System Boundaries and Primary vs. Secondary Actors
components.teaches: Students will learn how to construct clear system boundaries that separate internal automated behaviors from external user actions. They will classify primary actors, secondary supporting actors, and external third-party systems from informal text.

components.title: Standard Templates for Brief and Fully Dressed Use Cases
components.teaches: Students will compare standard use case templates, including Cockburn's casual and fully dressed formats. They will learn the mandatory fields required to document a use case brief concisely and unambiguously.

components.title: Extracting Use Cases from Unstructured Narrative Text
components.teaches: Students will apply a step-by-step heuristic to extract actor-goal pairs from informal user feedback and feature requests. They will learn how to filter out UI implementation details while retaining core functional requirements.

components.title: Formulating Main Success Scenarios with Strict Writing Guidelines
components.teaches: Students will learn standard grammatical rules for writing Main Success Scenario steps, such as using subject-verb-object structure, active voice, and explicit actor naming. They will convert informal step descriptions into standardized, sequential action steps.

components.title: Worked Example: Converting a Raw Feature Prompt to Use Case Outlines
components.teaches: Students will watch the step-by-step transformation of a multi-paragraph, messy product description for an e-commerce checkout into formal use case outlines. They will observe how to resolve ambiguous phrases, split compound goals, and establish system boundaries explicitly.

components.title: Specifying Preconditions, Guarantees, and Extension Branches
components.teaches: Students will learn how to formalize entry preconditions, minimal and success guarantees, and exception handling branches in standard use case documentation. They will evaluate trade-offs between detail level and specification maintainability.

components.title: Evaluating Use Case Quality and Completeness Checklist
components.teaches: Students will analyze sample use case outlines against a standard quality checklist to detect boundary leaks, missing actors, and untestable steps. They will discuss how standardized specifications reduce downstream errors in AI-assisted development.

components.title: Recap use case standards and spec guidelines
components.teaches: Students review the IEEE 830 and UML use case standards, and the spec-driven development guidelines for structuring requirements. They identify the mandatory elements of a use case specification.

components.title: Identify actors and system boundaries
components.teaches: Students learn a step‑by‑step method to extract actors, primary and secondary, and to draw the system boundary from a raw product description. They practice distinguishing internal vs. external actors.

components.title: Extract functional requirements from description
components.teaches: Using a worked example, students parse an unstructured product description to list functional requirements, grouping them by user goal. They apply a template to capture preconditions, postconditions, and triggers.

components.title: Write use case main success scenario
components.teaches: Students construct the main success scenario for a use case, writing numbered steps that show actor–system interactions. They ensure each step is atomic, observable, and follows the spec guidelines.

components.title: Write use case extensions and alternate flows
components.teaches: Students extend the main scenario with extension points, alternate flows, and exception handling, using the same numbering scheme. They learn to reference extension conditions and maintain traceability.

components.title: Create system boundary context diagram
components.teaches: In a live demo, the instructor builds a UML context diagram showing the system, actors, and external systems. Students see how the diagram validates the actor list and boundary decisions.

components.title: Prioritize use cases with MoSCoW
components.teaches: Students compare MoSCoW, business value, and risk‑based prioritization techniques on a sample use case set. They decide which use cases belong to Must, Should, Could, Won't for the first release.

components.title: Validate use cases against spec guidelines
components.teaches: Through guided discussion, students apply a checklist derived from spec‑driven guidelines to assess completeness, consistency, and testability of their use cases. They identify missing preconditions and ambiguous steps.

components.title: Map use cases to spec-driven framework artifacts
components.teaches: Students learn how each use case maps to downstream artifacts such as feature files, acceptance criteria, and test cases in a spec‑driven development framework. They trace a use case through the pipeline.

components.title: Case study: product description to use case model
components.teaches: A full case study walks through transforming a realistic product description into a complete use case model, including actors, boundary, scenarios, and prioritization. Students analyse each transformation decision.

components.title: Common pitfalls and quality checklist
components.teaches: Discussion of frequent errors such as actor overload, vague steps, and missing extensions. Students use a quality checklist to review a peer's use case specification and suggest improvements.

components.title: Summary and transition to spec-driven frameworks
components.teaches: Recap of the use case engineering process, emphasizing how the produced artifacts feed into spec‑driven development frameworks. Students outline next steps for automated test generation.

components.title: Foundations of Spec-Driven Development Frameworks
components.teaches: Students will understand the core workflow of spec-driven development (SDD) where formal specifications serve as the single source of truth prior to implementation. They will analyze how SDD differs from traditional Test-Driven Development (TDD) by decoupling interface contracts from language-specific test code. Students will also learn how LLMs and static analyzers leverage these frameworks to enforce architectural consistency.

components.title: Anatomy of Executable Specifications and Schemas
components.teaches: Students will examine the internal structural requirements of executable specifications using tools like OpenAPI, JSON Schema, or TypeSpec. They will learn how type definitions, input constraints, and response schemas define public interface signatures. Students will identify how machine-readable constraints enable automated contract validation before any code is generated.

components.title: Mapping Natural Language Requirements to Interface Contracts
components.teaches: Students will learn how to systematically convert informal, natural-language module requirements into structured interface contracts. The instructor demonstrates transforming ambiguous functional statements into unambiguous method signatures with specific parameters, return types, and exceptions. Students evaluate how precise specification bounds prevent runtime errors during code generation.

components.title: Specifying Preconditions, Postconditions, and Invariants
components.teaches: Students will formulate explicit invariants, preconditions, and postconditions for every public method in a target module using contract specification frameworks. They will construct concrete validation constraints for input parameters and standard return states. This ensures AI codegen tools generate implementation logic that strictly adheres to the specified contract.

components.title: Automated Test Generation from Executable Specifications
components.teaches: Students will observe how spec-driven frameworks automatically synthesize property-based tests and mock servers directly from specification definitions. The demonstration shows running executable specs against sample code to verify whether public methods conform to defined constraints. Students learn to interpret automated test failures resulting from specification violations.

components.title: Translating Complex Module Requirements into Executable Specifications
components.teaches: Students will follow a step-by-step translation of a multi-method business module's requirements into a complete, executable specification file. The worked example walks through defining request validation, error states, and public interface expectations for each method. Students see how to verify that every requirement maps directly to an executable check.

components.title: Mitigating Spec Drift and Handling Edge Cases
components.teaches: Students will analyze techniques for maintaining synchronization between evolving executable specifications and generated code over time. They will evaluate trade-offs in spec granularity, identifying when over-specifying hinders LLM code generation flexibility versus under-specifying causing contract breaches. Students discuss strategies to handle edge-case error scenarios within the spec framework.

M4.T2.topic: Requirements to executable specifications and code generation

components.title: Deconstructing Requirements into Public Method Contracts
components.teaches: Students will learn how to analyze informal requirements to identify public module methods, parameter contracts, and class invariants. They will establish strict preconditions, postconditions, and interface signatures needed before writing formal specifications.

components.title: Structuring Executable Specifications in Spec-Driven Frameworks
components.teaches: Students will learn the concrete syntax and structural conventions of spec-driven frameworks such as pytest-bdd or Behave. They will map high-level requirement statements into executable Given-When-Then scenario definitions tied directly to public API hooks.

components.title: Step-by-Step Translation of Requirements to Executable Specs
components.teaches: Students will follow a complete worked example translating a payment-processing requirement brief into an automated executable specification suite. They will observe how each requirement constraint is systematically formalized into assertion-backed test harnesses that cover all public methods.

components.title: Prompt Patterns for Generating Executable Specifications
components.teaches: Students will learn effective prompting architectures to instruct LLMs to synthesize spec-driven test suites from unstructured requirements documents. They will configure system instructions and interface schema definitions to eliminate hallucinations in method signatures and types.

components.title: Hands-on Authoring of Executable Specs from Requirements
components.teaches: Students will work in pairs to translate a natural-language requirement specification for a user session manager into an executable specification suite using a BDD framework. They will execute their specs against stub interfaces to confirm that every required public method is bounded by executable assertions.

components.title: Reviewing Spec Completeness and Interface Compliance
components.teaches: Students review criteria for determining whether an executable specification suite is fully complete and airtight before running code generation. They will inspect common edge-case omissions and parameter boundary failures that allow incorrect code to pass specifications.

components.title: Spec-Guided AI Code Generation and Validation Loop
components.teaches: Students will learn the automated feedback loop where LLMs consume executable specifications, generate implementation candidates, and refine code based on failing test traces. They will trace how automated test harness outputs act as prompt feedback to achieve zero interface violations.

components.title: Iterative Code Generation Against Executable Specifications
components.teaches: Students will use an AI assistant to generate production code that satisfies the executable specifications authored in the previous session. They will capture runtime test outputs, pass stack traces back to the model, and iteratively guide code generation until 100% of specification steps pass.

components.title: Comparing Conforming Implementations Against Spec Overfitting
components.teaches: Students will compare code that truly satisfies underlying business logic against code that overfits or cheats executable test mocks. They will evaluate techniques such as mutation testing and dynamic property checks to ensure generated code honors public method contracts.

components.title: Iterative Loop Engineering Overview
components.teaches: Students learn the definition of iterative loop engineering, its role in AI‑assisted coding, and the high‑level phases of a coding agent's generate‑test‑refactor cycle.

components.title: Execution Log Structure and Fields
components.teaches: Students identify the standard schema of an execution log, including timestamp, event type, agent identifier, and payload, and understand how each field maps to a control‑flow step.

components.title: Control‑Flow Step Taxonomy
components.teaches: Students categorize the distinct step types recorded in logs—function calls, loop iterations, conditional branches, and agent decision points—and explain how each appears in the log artifact.

components.title: Instrumentation and Logging Frameworks
components.teaches: Students observe a live demo of adding instrumentation hooks to a coding agent using Python's logging module and OpenTelemetry, seeing how logs are emitted in real time.

components.title: Worked Example: Simple Agent Loop Trace
components.teaches: Students follow a step‑by‑step trace of a toy generate‑test‑refactor agent, mapping each log entry to source‑code changes and identifying the control‑flow path.

components.title: Activity: Instrument a Toy Agent
components.teaches: Students modify a provided skeleton agent to emit structured logs, run it on a sample task, and verify that all control‑flow steps appear in the output log.

components.title: Mapping Log Steps to Code Changes
components.teaches: Students learn techniques to correlate log entries with diffs in the codebase, using timestamps and agent IDs to reconstruct the iterative development narrative.

components.title: Pitfalls and Best Practices in Tracing
components.teaches: Students compare common logging anti‑patterns—missing context, inconsistent granularity, and timestamp drift—with recommended practices for reliable traceability.

components.title: Recap: Log Schema and Step Types
components.teaches: Students quickly review the log schema and control‑flow taxonomy from the previous session to reinforce shared vocabulary before advanced topics.

components.title: Advanced Tracing: Nested and Parallel Loops
components.teaches: Students examine how nested iterative loops and concurrent agent executions appear in a single log, learning to disambiguate interleaved control‑flow steps using correlation IDs.

components.title: Worked Example: Real‑World Agent Log Analysis
components.teaches: Students walk through a full‑scale log from a production coding agent, extracting the generate‑test‑refactor cycles, identifying bottlenecks, and proposing instrumentation improvements.

components.title: Activity: Group Log Trace Report
components.teaches: In teams, students receive an anonymized iterative development log, produce a structured trace report linking each control‑flow step to code artifacts, and present findings.

M5.T2.topic: Iterative development logs and software factory outputs

components.title: Structure of iterative development logs
components.teaches: Students will understand the standard sections of an iterative development log (commit metadata, test results, tool invocations) and the schema of software factory output artifacts (build reports, artifact manifests).

components.title: Seeded defect taxonomy in factory outputs
components.teaches: Students will learn the four categories of seeded defects (missing dependency, flaky test, configuration drift, resource leak) and their characteristic signatures in logs and factory outputs.

components.title: Parsing and querying log data with CLI tools
components.teaches: Students will be able to use grep, jq, and custom scripts to extract relevant log entries and factory output fields for defect hunting.

components.title: Worked example: detecting a missing dependency defect
components.teaches: Students will follow a step‑by‑step analysis of a sample log where a missing dependency causes a build failure, seeing how to locate the error trace, correlate with the artifact manifest, and formulate a fix.

components.title: Activity: find two seeded defects in a provided log set
components.teaches: Students will individually examine a zip of logs and factory outputs, identify at least two of the four seeded defects, and write a brief fix proposal for each, then submit for peer review.

components.title: Comparing defect patterns across iterations
components.teaches: Students will compare how the same defect type manifests differently across multiple iterations, noting variations in log verbosity, test flakiness, and factory output anomalies.

components.title: Case study: real‑world factory log analysis
components.teaches: Students will review a redacted industry case where iterative logs revealed a configuration drift defect, discussing detection strategy, impact assessment, and remediation steps.

components.title: Discussion: best practices for proposing fixes
components.teaches: Students will evaluate fix proposals for completeness, testability, and regression risk, and agree on a checklist for future defect remediation in iterative loops.

M6.T1.topic: Software factories and execution trace analysis

components.title: Execution traces in software factories
components.teaches: Students learn what execution traces are, how coding agents emit them during iterative loop engineering, and why they are essential for diagnosing failures in software factories.

components.title: Log structure and iteration markers
components.teaches: Students examine the standardized format of iterative development logs, including timestamps, iteration IDs, tool calls, and error markers, enabling systematic navigation of up to 2000 lines.

components.title: Typical failure patterns in agent traces
components.teaches: Students identify three recurring failure categories—environment misconfiguration, dependency resolution errors, and logic regressions—and learn the trace signatures that distinguish each.

components.title: Trace collection and parsing tooling
components.teaches: Students watch a live demonstration of the factory's trace collector, log aggregator, and a Python script that parses raw logs into structured JSON for analysis.

components.title: Worked example: environment misconfiguration
components.teaches: Students follow a step‑by‑step analysis of a 500‑line trace, locating missing environment variables, correlating error codes, and citing exact log lines as evidence for the first failure cause.

components.title: Worked example: dependency resolution failure
components.teaches: Students trace a version conflict across iterations, observe repeated fetch retries, and extract the specific dependency graph lines that prove the second failure cause.

components.title: Worked example: logic regression detection
components.teaches: Students compare successive iteration outputs, spot a behavioral change in test results, and pinpoint the commit diff lines that constitute the third failure cause with supporting log excerpts.

components.title: Comparing failure causes across traces
components.teaches: Students contrast the three failure signatures side‑by‑side, evaluate their frequency and impact, and practice ranking them by severity using a structured rubric.

components.title: Activity: analyze full 2000‑line log
components.teaches: In pairs, students receive a 2000‑line factory log, apply the parsing script, identify at least three distinct failure causes, and record supporting log line numbers for each.

components.title: Discussion: reporting and best practices
components.teaches: Students present their findings, critique evidence quality, discuss how to automate failure‑cause detection, and outline a checklist for future trace analyses.

M6.T2.topic: Testing and validation in iterative development

components.title: Trace structure and metadata
components.teaches: Students learn the standard fields of an agent execution trace: timestamps, event types, tool calls, return values, and error codes. They understand how these fields map to the iterative loop steps and why consistent formatting matters for automated parsing.

components.title: Worked example: diagnosing tool misuse
components.teaches: The instructor walks through a 500-line trace where the agent repeatedly calls a file‑write tool with an invalid path. Students see how to locate the offending calls, correlate error codes, and confirm the root cause with log evidence.

components.title: Log parsing and query techniques
components.teaches: Students practice using grep, jq, and awk to filter a 2000-line trace for specific event types, extract timestamps, and count occurrences of error codes. They learn to build reusable one‑liners for rapid evidence gathering.

components.title: Systematic trace analysis workflow
components.teaches: A step‑by‑step method is introduced: (1) segment the trace by iteration, (2) hypothesize failure categories, (3) search for signature patterns, (4) collect supporting lines, (5) validate each hypothesis against the code context. Students apply the workflow to a short trace.

components.title: Worked example: multi-failure trace analysis
components.teaches: The instructor analyses a full 2000-line trace containing three distinct failures: a permission error, a version mismatch, and a logic loop. For each failure, the exact log lines are highlighted and linked to the underlying cause.

components.title: Activity: pair analysis of new trace
components.teaches: In pairs, students receive a fresh 1500-line trace and must identify at least three failure causes, citing line numbers and error codes. They prepare a brief report and present findings to the class for peer review.

components.title: Comparison of analysis strategies
components.teaches: Students compare manual trace inspection, scripted querying, and LLM‑assisted summarisation. They evaluate speed, accuracy, and false‑positive rates on the same trace, discussing when each approach is preferable.

components.title: Discussion: validation and reporting findings
components.teaches: The class discusses how to validate identified causes (re‑run, unit test, stakeholder confirmation) and how to structure a concise failure report for developers. Emphasis is placed on actionable recommendations and traceability back to log evidence.

components.title: AI-native architectures and testing challenges
components.teaches: Students will identify the distinctive characteristics of AI-native software (data‑driven behavior, non‑determinism, model drift) and explain why traditional testing approaches fall short. They will list at least three testing challenges unique to AI components.

components.title: Unit testing mechanisms for ML models
components.teaches: Students will describe property‑based testing, metamorphic testing, and model‑behavior contracts as unit‑level mechanisms for ML models. They will apply one mechanism to a sample classifier and articulate the trade‑off between coverage and oracle cost.

components.title: Integration testing for AI pipelines
components.teaches: Students will explain contract testing, data‑drift detection, and end‑to‑end pipeline validation as integration mechanisms. They will compare how each mechanism handles versioned models and evolving data schemas.

components.title: Model quality evaluation metrics
components.teaches: Students will define accuracy, fairness, robustness, and calibration metrics and explain when each is appropriate for AI-native systems. They will compute a fairness disparity metric on a provided confusion matrix.

components.title: System-level evaluation metrics
components.teaches: Students will describe latency, throughput, cost, and reliability metrics for deployed AI services. They will analyse a scenario to decide which system‑level metric dominates the testing budget.

components.title: Comparative framework for testing selection
components.teaches: Students will use a decision matrix (mechanism vs. metric vs. risk) to compare and select appropriate testing mechanisms and evaluation metrics for a given AI-native architecture. They will justify their choices with respect to risk tolerance and resource constraints.

components.title: Case study: applying comparison framework
components.teaches: Students will walk through a realistic AI‑native service (e.g., a recommendation API) and apply the comparative framework to choose testing mechanisms and metrics. They will evaluate the completeness of their selection and suggest improvements.

components.title: AI-Native Testing Landscape Overview
components.teaches: Students will identify the unique challenges of testing AI-native systems, including nondeterminism, data drift, and model versioning. They will distinguish between model-centric and system-centric testing concerns.

components.title: Unit Testing ML Model Components
components.teaches: Students will describe unit-level testing mechanisms such as property-based testing, metamorphic testing, and test oracle construction for individual model functions. They will explain how these mechanisms detect logic errors in preprocessing, inference, and postprocessing.

components.title: Integration Testing of ML Pipelines
components.teaches: Students will outline integration testing strategies for end-to-end ML pipelines, including contract testing, schema validation, and pipeline replay. They will compare static vs dynamic pipeline validation approaches.

components.title: Model Performance Evaluation Metrics
components.teaches: Students will define key model-centric metrics such as accuracy, F1, AUC, calibration error, and perplexity, and explain when each is appropriate. They will interpret metric trade-offs for classification, generation, and ranking tasks.

components.title: System-Level Quality Metrics
components.teaches: Students will describe system-level metrics including latency, throughput, memory footprint, robustness to adversarial inputs, and data freshness. They will relate these metrics to SLA requirements in production AI services.

components.title: Mapping Mechanisms to Metrics
components.teaches: Students will apply a comparative framework that links each testing mechanism to the metrics it informs, highlighting coverage gaps. They will evaluate which combination of mechanisms yields comprehensive metric coverage for a given architecture.

components.title: Case Study: RAG Pipeline Evaluation
components.teaches: Students will walk through a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, applying unit, integration, and system tests, and compute model and system metrics. They will critique the evaluation plan and suggest improvements.

M8.T1.topic: Reliable and safe trustworthy software architectures

components.title: AI-native factory pipeline architecture overview
components.teaches: Students will understand the high-level structure of an AI-native software factory, identifying the major pipeline components such as data ingestion, model training, validation, and deployment. They will recognize how these components interact to form an end-to-end automated workflow.

components.title: Automated testing stages in AI pipelines
components.teaches: Students will learn the concrete testing stages used in AI-native pipelines: unit tests for code, integration tests for data flows, model validation tests (accuracy, fairness), and data drift detection. They will be able to describe the purpose and typical tooling for each stage.

components.title: Mapping reliability requirements to pipeline stages
components.teaches: Students will analyse a set of reliability requirements (e.g., reproducibility, latency, fault tolerance) and map each requirement to specific pipeline stages and testing mechanisms. They will compare how different requirements influence test design choices.

components.title: Worked example: assessing sample pipeline reliability
components.teaches: Through a guided walkthrough, students will evaluate a provided sample AI pipeline against a list of reliability requirements, justifying each assessment decision with concrete evidence from the pipeline's test configuration. They will practice the evaluation criteria needed for the final assessment.

components.title: Recap: pipeline assessment criteria discussion
components.teaches: Students will briefly revisit the assessment criteria and reliability requirement mappings covered previously, clarifying any gaps through instructor-led discussion. This sets the context for deeper analysis of a multi-component project.

components.title: Defining reliability requirements for multi-component AI
components.teaches: Students will learn how to elicit and formalize reliability requirements for a system composed of multiple AI services (e.g., service-level objectives, error budgets, cascade failure policies). They will apply a template to a supplied project description.

components.title: Case study: industry AI pipeline reliability
components.teaches: Students will examine a real-world case study of an AI-native pipeline in production, focusing on how the organization defined reliability requirements, instrumented testing stages, and measured outcomes. They will analyse trade-offs made by the team.

components.title: Worked example: assessing supplied project pipeline
components.teaches: The instructor demonstrates a full assessment of the supplied multi-component software project's testing pipeline, linking each design decision to a specific reliability requirement and showing how to document justifications. Students follow the reasoning step by step.

components.title: Group activity: assess pipeline and justify
components.teaches: In small groups, students receive a different pipeline configuration for the same project and must assess it against the reliability requirements, producing a written justification for each design decision. Groups present findings for peer review.

components.title: Trade-offs: testing depth vs deployment speed
components.teaches: Students will compare the impact of increasing test coverage and rigor on deployment latency and resource consumption. They will evaluate scenarios where faster deployment may be preferred over exhaustive testing, supporting arguments with metrics.

components.title: Key deployment metrics overview
components.teaches: Students learn the definitions of latency, error rate, throughput, deployment frequency, and rollback time. They understand how each metric signals the health of a deployment pipeline.

components.title: Reliability metrics and SLOs
components.teaches: Students define availability, MTBF, MTTR, SLO, SLI, and error budget. They see how these metrics quantify system reliability and guide release decisions.

components.title: Instrumenting a multi-component system with OpenTelemetry
components.teaches: Students follow the steps to add traces, metrics, and logs across services using OpenTelemetry SDKs. They configure exporters to Prometheus and verify that data flows correctly.

components.title: Live dashboard walkthrough with Grafana
components.teaches: Students watch the creation of a Grafana dashboard that visualizes deployment and reliability metrics. They learn to set alert rules on error‑budget burn rate.

components.title: Scenario walkthrough 1: load‑test and failure injection
components.teaches: The instructor runs a k6 load test against the sample project, injects a service failure with Chaos Mesh, and evaluates whether SLOs remain satisfied. Students observe metric shifts in real time.

components.title: Student activity: evaluate metrics on supplied project
components.teaches: In pairs, students use the instrumented project to compute deployment and reliability metrics, decide if a release meets the defined SLOs, and present their go/no‑go recommendation for peer review.

components.title: Comparing scenario walkthroughs: lessons learned
components.teaches: A brief recap of the first walkthrough is followed by a comparison with a second scenario (canary vs. blue‑green). Students analyse how metric patterns differ and what that implies for rollback decisions.

components.title: Scenario walkthrough 2: canary deployment evaluation
components.teaches: The instructor demonstrates a live canary rollout, monitors the error budget in Grafana, makes a go/no‑go decision, and documents the evaluation for a post‑mortem. Students practice the full evaluation loop.
